other_texts.ref: Maimonides, Epistle to Yemen (Iggeret Teiman), Cohen tr., section X

response_by: Maimonides (Epistle to Yemen) - a Jewish response used by Christians too
arguments.response: Respondents point to the parallel verse, 18:15: God will raise up a prophet 'from among you, of your brothers'. In Deuteronomy 'your brothers' regularly means fellow Israelites; the king must be 'one from among your brothers', not 'a foreigner' (17:15). Maimonides (12th century) says the phrase 'from the midst of thee' was added precisely so that 'brethren' could not be taken to include Esau or Ishmael. He also notes that 'like unto me' cannot mean equal to Moses, since 'there has not arisen a prophet since in Israel like Moses' (34:10). Christians add that Acts 3:22 applies the verse to Jesus, and that John 1:21 shows a single 'Prophet' was expected within Israel.
arguments.facts: Checkable: 18:15 says 'from among you, of your brothers' and 18:18 'from among their brothers'. 17:15 uses 'brother' to mean a fellow Israelite as opposed to 'a foreigner', while Numbers 20:14 calls Edom (Esau) Israel's 'brother'. Deuteronomy 34:10 says no prophet like Moses had arisen 'in Israel'. Interpretation: the list of Moses-Muhammad likenesses is selective in both directions (Jesus also gave a law-like teaching, was rejected and so on).
arguments.assessment: The 'brothers' argument is the weak point: within Deuteronomy the nearest parallel (17:15) and 18:15's 'from among you' point to Israelites, as both Jewish and Christian commentators note. Deedat's likeness list is clever but depends on which traits one picks. Deuteronomy 34:10 shows that 'a prophet like Moses' was an open expectation, which is why both Christians and Muslims claim the verse; it is not the Muslim argument's strong point.

arguments.title: Is the Paraclete Jesus promised in John 14-16 a prophecy of Muhammad?

favours.text: On this question the Christian side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim argument has not shown what it claims.

arguments.argument: Jesus promises 'another Counselor' (parakletos) who will come only after he goes away (John 14:16; 16:7). The Paraclete will guide into all truth and 'not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak' (16:13). Quran 61:6 says Jesus announced 'a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad'. Deedat and earlier Keldani argued that the original Greek was periklytos ('praised one', in Arabic Ahmad), later changed to parakletos. They also argue that the Holy Spirit was already active before Jesus left, so the condition 'if I don't go away, the Counselor won't come' fits a later human prophet better.
response_by: Wikipedia summary citing Guthrie & Bishop, W. Montgomery Watt and Sean Anthony
arguments.response: No known Greek manuscript reads periklytos; all read parakletos, and the evidence goes back to the 3rd century. The text itself identifies the Paraclete: 'the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name' (John 14:26), 'the Spirit of truth... he lives with you, and will be in you' (14:17), whom 'the world can't receive' because it 'doesn't see him'. These are hard to apply to a human prophet born six centuries later. Historically, according to Sean Anthony, Ibn Ishaq does not link the passage to Ahmad; the connection first appears in Ibn Hisham and Ibn Qutayba.
arguments.facts: Checkable: all Greek manuscripts read parakletos; John 14:26 names the Paraclete as 'the Holy Spirit', and 14:17 says he 'lives with you, and will be in you'. 61:6 does contain the name 'Ahmad'. Interpretation: the periklytos theory is a conjecture without manuscript support; whether 16:7's 'if I go' condition fits the Spirit is a theological question answered by John 7:39-type passages (not checked here).
arguments.assessment: This is one of the weakest Muslim arguments on the texts. The proposed original reading has no manuscript support, and the passage explicitly calls the Paraclete the Holy Spirit, invisible to the world and indwelling the disciples. The argument survives only if one assumes the text was altered at exactly this point, which is the conclusion it needs to prove.

arguments.title: Is it unjust for an innocent man to die for others' sins, given Ezekiel 18:20?

favours.text: Evenly balanced: each side has real texts on its side, and neither has disproved the other.

by: Shabir Ally (debate with James White, Seattle, 19 Oct 2007, and follow-up articles, as quoted by Shamoun)
arguments.argument: 'The soul who sins, he shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son' (Ezekiel 18:20; cf. Deuteronomy 24:16). The Quran says the same many times: 'no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another' (6:164, 17:15, 35:18, 39:7). Muslims argue that punishing a sinless person in place of the guilty is unjust by the Bible's own standard. They also argue that inherited guilt from Adam (Romans 5:12) is excluded by Ezekiel 18, and that God forgives the repentant directly (Ezekiel 18:21-23). When James White answered with 'corporate justice', citing Achan's family being stoned with him (Joshua 7), Ally replied that this was simply another injustice: 'Two wrongs do not make a right.'

texts.note: verse 25 checked

arguments.response: Wood replies that Ezekiel 18 forbids punishing children for parents' crimes against their will; it does not rule out a willing substitute who takes on the penalty, which the same Hebrew Bible foresees (Isaiah 53:5, 'he was pierced for our transgressions'; Leviticus 17:11). He argues the Quran is not consistent here either. It says misleaders will carry 'burdens along with their own burdens' (29:13; 16:25). And Sahih Muslim 2767 says that on the Day of Resurrection God will hand each Muslim a Jew or Christian and say 'That is your rescue from Hell-Fire'. If the Quran's principle allows that, Wood argues, it cannot rule out a sinless volunteer dying for sinners. White argues that the Bible knows corporate as well as individual responsibility (Achan), so the objection assumes a purely individualist model of justice.
arguments.facts: Checkable: Ezekiel 18:20 and the Quranic 'no bearer of burdens' verses say what is quoted. Isaiah 53:5 and Leviticus 17:11 speak of atonement through another's suffering or blood. Quran 29:13 and 16:25 speak of misleaders bearing others' burdens, and Muslim 2767 does say Jews and Christians will be a Muslim's 'rescue' (fikak) from the Fire. Interpretation: Muslim scholars generally read 29:13 as the misleaders' own sin of misleading, and Muslim 2767 as the unbeliever taking his own place in Hell, not a Muslim's punishment; those readings were not checked in a source read here.
arguments.assessment: Both sides have a fair point. Ezekiel 18 is about human justice and inherited guilt, so it does not squarely address voluntary substitution, which weakens the Muslim proof-text. But penal substitution is philosophically contested even among Christians, and the Muslim intuition that guilt cannot be transferred is widely shared. Wood's appeal to Muslim 2767 is a sharp counterpoint, though it depends on a reading of that hadith that Muslims dispute.

arguments.title: Do Old Testament commands to destroy whole peoples undermine Christian moral objections to Islam?

favours.text: On this question the Muslim side makes more sense on the texts. The Christian replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Ali Ataie (debate with David Wood, per review)
arguments.argument: When Christian apologists criticize violence in Muhammad's career, Muslim debaters such as Ataie answer by pointing to the 'violent verses' of the Bible. God commands Saul: 'go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have... kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby' (1 Samuel 15:3). Of Canaanite cities: 'you shall save alive nothing that breathes' (Deuteronomy 20:16). After the Midianite war, Moses orders the killing of every male child and every non-virgin woman (Numbers 31:17). The argument is that Christians who accept these as God's commands cannot consistently condemn Muhammad's wars or the Banu Qurayza judgment as proof he was not a prophet.
response_by: Paul Copan (Is God a Moral Monster?, 2011)
arguments.response: Copan argues that the 'utterly destroy' (herem) language is conventional ancient Near Eastern war hyperbole. The same term is used of Judah in Jeremiah 25:9, yet the book goes on to describe many survivors. He notes that Amalekites appear again soon after 1 Samuel 15 (1 Samuel 27:8; 30:1). He argues that the commands were limited to a specific time and place, not ongoing rules, that they were judgments on particular wickedness rather than ethnic hatred, and that Israel was warned it would be judged in the same way. Wood, by contrast, argues that the Quran commands ongoing fighting (for example 9:29), so the cases are not parallel.
arguments.facts: Checkable: 1 Samuel 15:3, Deuteronomy 20:16 and Numbers 31:17 contain the commands quoted. Amalekites appear raiding again in 1 Samuel 27:8 and 30:1, and Jeremiah 25:9 uses 'utterly destroy' of Judah, which survives. Quran 9:29 commands fighting certain People of the Book until they pay the jizya. Interpretation: whether herem is hyperbole and whether the Quranic commands are bounded or general are disputed by scholars on each side.
arguments.assessment: As a consistency argument (tu quoque) this is effective: both scriptures contain divinely commanded warfare, and neither tradition can treat violence as proof of the other's falsehood without explaining its own texts. It does not show either set of texts is morally acceptable. Copan's hyperbole defence has textual support (Amalekite survivors) but critics say it does not remove the moral problem of the command itself.

arguments.title: Does Isaiah 7:14 predict a virgin birth, or a young woman's child in King Ahaz's day?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Christian replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld (Aish.com), pointing readers to Rabbi Tovia Singer
arguments.argument: Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 as 'the virgin shall be with child', but the Hebrew word is almah, which means a young woman without regard to virginity. Hebrew has a specific word for virgin, betulah, which Isaiah does not use, and Proverbs 30:19 uses almah where a sexual relationship is in view. Isaiah says 'the' young woman, a specific woman Ahaz could identify. The sign is tied to Ahaz's crisis: before the child knows good from evil, the two kings Ahaz fears will be gone (7:16). A birth seven centuries later could not reassure Ahaz, and in any case a virgin birth could not serve as a visible sign.

texts.note: JPS: 'the young woman is with child'; WEB: 'the virgin will conceive'
JPS: 'how a man has his way with a maiden'

response_by: Michael L. Brown (Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus vol. 3, as summarized by Jews for Jesus)
arguments.response: Brown concedes that almah 'does not specifically mean virgin'; its basic sense is a young woman of marriageable age. But he argues that betulah is also not a strictly technical word for virgin (Jews for Jesus summarizes his detailed case in vol. 3, section 4.3), and that in Isaiah's culture a young unmarried almah would be presumed to be a virgin. The Septuagint, made by Jewish translators before Christianity, rendered almah here as parthenos ('virgin'), so Matthew follows an existing Jewish reading. Christian interpreters also connect the child named Immanuel ('God with us') to the royal child of 9:6 ('Mighty God'), arguing for a fulfilment beyond Ahaz's time, though many accept a first, near fulfilment in Isaiah's day.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the Hebrew has ha-almah ('the young woman'), not betulah; the LXX has parthenos; Matthew 1:23 follows the Greek. Isaiah 7:16 ties the sign to the defeat of Ahaz's enemies before the child knows good and evil. Interpretation: whether a double or later fulfilment is allowed, and how much parthenos tells us about the meaning of the Hebrew, are disputed.
arguments.assessment: On the Hebrew and the immediate context, the Jewish reading is stronger: almah does not specify virginity, and the sign is framed for Ahaz's lifetime, as most modern translations and many Christian scholars accept. The Christian case rests mainly on the Septuagint and on reading Isaiah 7-11 as a messianic unit. Those are real arguments, but they belong to how Matthew read Isaiah more than to what Isaiah 7:14 says on its own.

arguments.title: Is the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 the nation of Israel or the Messiah?

favours.text: Evenly balanced: each side has real texts on its side, and neither has disproved the other.

arguments.argument: Singer argues that Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 is the fourth of the Servant Songs, and the earlier songs name the servant explicitly as Israel/Jacob (41:8-9, 44:1, 44:21, 45:4, 49:3). The speakers in chapter 53 are the astonished 'kings' of 52:15, who in the messianic age confess that they despised Israel and that its suffering came from their own wickedness. He says this is the prevailing rabbinic reading (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi, Nachmanides and others). He also notes that it is not a medieval invention: Origen (c. 248) reported that Jews of his day applied the passage to 'the whole people, regarded as one individual'.

texts.note: 'the leper of the house of Rabbi' quoting Isaiah 53:4

other_texts.note: quoted by Singer; not checked

response_by: Jews for Jesus ('Isaiah 53: A Definitive Messianic Guide')
arguments.response: Christian respondents point out that ancient Jewish sources also read the passage messianically. Targum Jonathan identifies the servant as the Messiah. The Babylonian Talmud says the rabbis gave the Messiah's name as 'the leper of the house of Rabbi', quoting Isaiah 53:4 (Sanhedrin 98b). Maimonides' Epistle to Yemen is also listed by the Wikipedia summary among messianic readings. Textually, the servant is innocent ('he had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth', 53:9) and suffers 'for the disobedience of my people' (53:8), while Isaiah elsewhere calls Israel 'a sinful nation' (1:4). Christians argue that this distinguishes the servant from the nation he suffers for.
arguments.facts: Checkable: earlier Servant Songs explicitly call the servant 'Israel' (49:3). Isaiah 53:8-9 describes the servant as innocent and stricken 'for the disobedience of my people'. Targum Jonathan and Sanhedrin 98b apply parts of the passage to the Messiah, and Origen reports a national reading among Jews in the 3rd century. Interpretation: both national and individual readings are ancient within Judaism; Christian identification with Jesus rests on New Testament usage (Acts 8:32-35).
arguments.assessment: Both sides can cite early Jewish evidence, so neither 'the messianic reading is a Christian invention' nor 'the national reading is a medieval reaction to Christianity' holds up. The national reading has the strongest support from the surrounding chapters; the individual reading has the strongest support from 53:8-9, where the servant suffers for 'my people'. The site should present this as a genuine exegetical dispute.

arguments.title: Did Jesus fail the Jewish criteria for the Messiah (Temple, ingathering, peace)?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Christian replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Rabbi Tovia Singer (quoted by Luke Lancaster, Catholic Answers)
Rabbi Yitzchak Breitowitz (as cited by Lancaster)
arguments.argument: Maimonides gives the test: a king from the house of David who studies Torah, keeps the commandments, leads Israel in observance and fights God's wars may be presumed to be the Messiah. If he succeeds, builds the Temple in its place and gathers the dispersed of Israel, he is definitely the Messiah. Jesus did none of these. He did not rebuild the Temple, which was destroyed in 70 CE; he did not gather the exiles; and the world-wide peace promised in Isaiah 2:4 did not come. Singer: 'If Jesus were the Messiah, you would know it from reading the newspaper.' Breitowitz adds that Jesus set aside parts of the Torah (Mark 7:19), which the Messiah may not do (Deuteronomy 30:16), and a Messiah who dies at the hands of Rome has failed.
response_by: Michael L. Brown (Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus vol. 1)
arguments.response: Christians answer that the prophecies do not say they must all be fulfilled in one coming. Jesus implied that the promises of peace would be fulfilled at his return (Matthew 24), and some Jewish texts also expected a Messiah who first suffers and later triumphs. The new covenant was expected to differ from the Sinai covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-32), so changes to the Torah are not automatically disqualifying. Daniel 9:26 says an anointed one will be 'cut off', which Lancaster (following Brant Pitre and John Collins) takes as a Hebrew idiom for being put to death. Isaiah 53 is read as foretelling a dying servant. The twelve apostles are read as the start of the regathering of the twelve tribes (Luke 22:30).
arguments.facts: Checkable: Maimonides' criteria in Kings 11:4 are as quoted (Davidic king, Torah observance, rebuilding the Temple, ingathering of exiles). The Temple was destroyed in 70 CE and has not been rebuilt. Jeremiah 31:31 promises a 'new covenant'. Interpretation: whether the Messiah's work may be split across two comings is the crux, and the Hebrew Bible does not explicitly describe a second coming.
arguments.assessment: On the plain criteria held in mainstream rabbinic Judaism, the Jewish objection is strong: the defining public acts of the Messianic age have not happened. The Christian reply (two comings) is internally consistent but is a reinterpretation that the Hebrew Bible does not state outright. It depends on prior acceptance of Jesus's resurrection. This argument therefore mostly measures each tradition's definition of 'Messiah' rather than settling the question.

arguments.title: Does the Torah foretell Muhammad as the 'prophet from among your brethren'?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim replies have not overturned it so far.

arguments.argument: Muslims, from medieval polemicists to Deedat, argue that Deuteronomy 18:15-18 and the Quran's claim that Muhammad is 'written in the Torah' (7:157) point to an Arab prophet from the Israelites' 'brethren', the Ishmaelites. Maimonides answers that the verse must be read in context: it follows bans on divination and promises Israel a prophet who will live 'in the midst of thee'. 'From the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me' means a Jew. The words were added because 'of thy brethren' alone might have been misunderstood to include Esau or Ishmael, since Israel calls Edom 'brother' (Numbers 20:14). 'Like unto me' does not mean equal to Moses, since 'there hath not arisen a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses' (34:10), and the prophet foretold is not one who brings a new law.
response_by: The apostate Maimonides was answering (identified by Haggai Mazuz as al-Samaw'al al-Maghribi, author of Ifham al-Yahud)
arguments.response: Deedat argues that if the prophet were to be an Israelite the text would say 'from among yourselves', and that 18:18 says 'from among their brethren'. In his reading Israel's brethren are Ishmael's descendants, Abraham's other line, and Muhammad matches Moses in birth, marriage, family, leadership, law-giving and natural death. He reads Deuteronomy 34:10 ('there has not arisen... in Israel') as showing the prophet would arise outside Israel. The anonymous Jewish apostate whom Maimonides answered (possibly al-Samaw'al al-Maghribi, a 12th-century convert to Islam) used selected Torah passages in the same way.
arguments.facts: Checkable: 18:15 says 'from the midst of thee, of thy brethren' and 18:18 'from among their brethren'. Deuteronomy uses 'brother' for fellow Israelites (17:15) and once calls Edom Israel's 'brother' (Numbers 20:14). 34:10 says no prophet like Moses had arisen 'in Israel'. The Quran claims Muhammad is described in the Torah (7:157) but does not cite Deuteronomy 18. Interpretation: the identity of the promised prophet is read differently by Jews (a line of Israelite prophets), Christians (Jesus, Acts 3:22) and Muslims (Muhammad).
arguments.assessment: Maimonides' contextual argument is strong. 18:15's 'from the midst of thee' and the use of 'brother' in 17:15 make an Israelite referent the natural reading. The Muslim reading depends mainly on 18:18 taken in isolation and on a selective list of likenesses. The Quran's general claim (7:157) is a theological statement that cannot be checked against a specific Torah verse.

arguments.title: Did Jews ever call Ezra ('Uzayr) the son of God, as Quran 9:30 says?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Encyclopaedia Judaica and the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia (as summarized in Wikipedia 'Uzair')
arguments.argument: Quran 9:30 says: 'The Jews say, Ezra is the son of Allah; and the Christians say, The Messiah is the son of Allah.' Jewish scholars object that no such belief is found anywhere in Jewish literature. Ezra is honoured as the scribe who restored the Torah, but never as divine or as God's son. The Encyclopaedia Judaica calls the Quranic statement 'an enigma' for this reason. The 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia suggests it is a hostile metaphor for Jewish reverence for Ezra. The objection is that the Quran attributes to Jews a belief they did not hold.
response_by: Ibn Hazm (as reported by Ibrahim Awad)
Shorter Jewish Encyclopedia / H. Z. Hirschberg (Yemenite-Jewish hypothesis)
arguments.response: Ibn Kathir simply takes the verse as reporting what (some) Jews claimed. Ibn Hazm, according to Ibrahim Awad, attributed the belief to a Sadducee group in Yemen. Gordon Newby suggests that Jews of the Hijaz may have counted Ezra among the 'Bene Elohim' ('sons of God') because of his piety, possibly linked to mystical traditions identifying Ezra with Enoch or Metatron (3 Enoch). The Shorter Jewish Encyclopedia and Hirschberg suggest a local Yemenite oral tradition, perhaps linked to 2 Esdras, in which Ezra was regarded as messianic. Muslim interpreters stress that the verse concerns a particular group known to the Prophet, not all Jews at all times.
arguments.facts: Checkable: 9:30 states that 'the Jews' say Ezra is the son of God. Mainstream Jewish literature known today contains no such belief, as Jewish reference works say. The explanations offered (Yemenite or Hijazi sects, Enoch-Metatron speculation) are hypotheses without direct documentary evidence of Jews calling Ezra God's son. Interpretation: whether 'the Jews' means all Jews or a specific local group is a reading of the verse.
arguments.assessment: The Jewish objection is strong on the evidence: no Jewish text calls Ezra the son of God, and the Muslim and academic explanations are conjectures about lost local groups. The best Muslim reply is that the verse may refer to a small, now-unattested group in 7th-century Arabia, which cannot be disproven but also cannot be shown. The site should state the textual fact clearly and present the explanations as hypotheses.

arguments.title: Does the Shema ('the LORD is one') rule out the Trinity and a God who becomes man?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Christian replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Maimonides (Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7-8, 1:11)
arguments.argument: Deuteronomy 6:4, 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD is our God, the LORD is one (echad)', is Judaism's central creed. Singer argues that Christians who read echad as a 'compound unity' cite only verses where 'one' covers several things, such as one cluster of grapes (Numbers 13:23) or one day (Genesis 1:5). The same word also means one alone: one witness (Deuteronomy 17:6, 19:15) and 'one alone, without a companion; he has neither son nor brother' (Ecclesiastes 4:8). For Singer, 'the Lord is one' is 'unsullied monotheism'. Maimonides adds that God is one with a unity unlike any in the world, 'not one in the manner of a general category which includes many individual entities'. God has no body: Maimonides cites Deuteronomy 4:15 ('you saw no shape') and Isaiah 40:25 ('To whom can you liken Me?'), and says death and other bodily states do not apply to God. On this view a God who becomes a man and dies is excluded. Jewish writers also cite 'I am God, not man' (Hosea 11:9) and 'God is not a man' (Numbers 23:19).

texts.note: JPS renders 'a first day'; Hebrew yom echad
'one flesh' (basar echad), cited by Christians for a composite 'one'

other_texts.ref: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:7
Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:8
Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:11
Hasagot HaRaavad on Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:7
other_texts.note: Raavad objects to calling believers in a corporeal God heretics, since 'many greater and better than he' held that view

response_by: Brian J. Wright (Christian Research Journal, republished by equip.org)
New Testament texts (Mark 12:29; 1 Corinthians 8:6; John 1:14, 18; Colossians 2:9)
arguments.response: Wright reads the Shema as a covenant statement: 'a covenant relationship with one God inside of one covenant community'. He notes that Jesus himself quotes the Shema as the greatest commandment (Mark 12:29) and that Paul repeats it with 'one God, the Father ... and one Lord, Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 8:6). So Christians claim to affirm the Shema while holding that 'our understanding of the inner nature of this one God is clearer, sharper, and more precise'. He also cites Genesis 2:24 ('one flesh') as an example of echad describing a composite unity. On the incarnation, the Christian reply comes from the New Testament itself: 'No one has seen God at any time' (John 1:18), yet 'the Word became flesh' (John 1:14), and the fullness of deity dwells in him 'bodily' (Colossians 2:9). Christians argue that Deuteronomy 4:15 forbids Israel to make images because it saw no form at Sinai; it does not say what God may do later. I did not find a named Christian writer making this specific reply to Deuteronomy 4:15 in a source I could read.
arguments.facts: Checkable: Deuteronomy 6:4 reads YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad. Echad is used both for a single thing (one witness; Ecclesiastes 4:8) and for one thing made of parts (one cluster; one flesh), so the word alone neither requires nor excludes distinctions within God. Deuteronomy 4:15 says Israel saw no shape at Horeb and draws a ban on images from that. Hosea 11:9 says 'I am God, not man' in a passage about God holding back his anger, and Numbers 23:19 says God does not lie or change his mind. Neither verse is directly about incarnation. Maimonides counts belief in a corporeal God as heresy (Repentance 3:7), but his contemporary Raavad objected that many greater scholars had held it. Incorporeality as a binding doctrine is therefore Maimonides' formulation, not a view all Jews held before him. Interpretation: whether the Shema's 'one' rules out persons within God is a question of theology, not of vocabulary.
arguments.assessment: The vocabulary argument is weak on both sides. Singer is right that echad does not mean 'compound unity', and Christians are right that it does not mean 'absolutely simple' either. The Jewish case is stronger when it leaves vocabulary aside. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly insists that God has no rival and no likeness (Isaiah 40:25, 44:6), and nothing in it teaches a Trinity or a God who becomes human. Christians must rely on New Testament revelation for both doctrines. The Christian reply shows that Trinitarians affirm the Shema rather than reject it; it does not show that the Shema teaches the Trinity. Maimonides' incorporeality argument is rigorous, but it is a philosophical system, and Raavad's gloss shows it was contested within Judaism. A fair verdict is that the Shema fits Jewish unitarian monotheism most naturally, but does not by itself refute the Christian claim.

arguments.title: Does Psalm 22:16 say 'they pierced my hands and feet', or 'like a lion, my hands and feet'?

favours.text: Evenly balanced: each side has real texts on its side, and neither has disproved the other.

arguments.argument: Christian Bibles translate Psalm 22:16 (22:17 in Hebrew numbering) as 'they pierced my hands and my feet' and read it as a prophecy of the crucifixion. Kravitz argues that the Hebrew word is ka'ari, 'like a lion', the same form that is translated 'like a lion' in Isaiah 38:13, Numbers 24:9 and Ezekiel 22:25. He says Christian Bibles translate it differently only here. The psalm keeps comparing David's enemies to animals that surround him: bulls (v. 13), a tearing and roaring lion (v. 14), dogs (v. 17). The phrase therefore means 'like a lion [they are at] my hands and my feet', with the verb left implied, as Hebrew often does. Rashi explains it as 'as though they are crushed in a lion's mouth', citing Hezekiah's 'like a lion, so it would break all my bones' (Isaiah 38:13). Kravitz also argues that the Septuagint's 'they dug' may come from misreading the Hebrew. In his view the Nahal Hever scroll's spelling with a vav still keeps the aleph of 'lion', and that scribe often wrote yod so that it looks like vav. He adds that crucifixion was common, so the verse could not single out one person anyway.

texts.note: Hebrew ka'ari
Greek oryxan, 'they dug'; Brenton edition (ebible.org)

other_texts.note: Masoretic text reads ka'ari
Aramaic reads 'biting like a lion my hands and feet', which supplies a verb; read in Aramaic on Sefaria
reading k'rw reported by Kravitz and Hegg; not seen by me
cited by Hegg; not checked

arguments.response: Hegg argues that the Greek Septuagint translated the word as oryxan ('they dug' or 'they pierced'), so the translator was reading a different Hebrew word. He says a Hebrew fragment from Nahal Hever, which he dates to 50-68 CE, spells the word with a final vav: 'The word clearly ended in a vav not a yod, and was therefore a 3rd person plural verb.' He cites Ben Chayim's Masorah Finalis: 'In some correct Codices I have found כארו as the Ketiv and כארי as the Qeri.' He also argues that 'like a lion my hands and my feet' seems to lack a verb, and that the Targum's addition of a verb shows the difficulty. Hopkin's BYU Studies article frames the issue the same way. Everything turns on one letter: with a vav (כארו) 'pierced/dug' is tenable; with a yod (כארי) the Masoretic 'like a lion' results. He lists modern translations that go each way.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the Masoretic text has כָּאֲרִי, the form meaning 'like a lion' elsewhere (Isaiah 38:13; Numbers 24:9; Ezekiel 22:25). The Greek Psalter reads ὤρυξαν, 'they dug'. The Aramaic Targum reads 'biting like a lion my hands and feet'. So the Jewish Aramaic translator read 'lion' but still added a verb, which supports both Kravitz's lion reading and Hegg's point that the phrase is elliptical. Not checked by me: the Nahal Hever reading and Ben Chayim's Masorah note. Interpretation: whether כארו (if that is the reading) is a verb or a variant spelling of 'like a lion' is disputed. 'Dug' is not the usual Hebrew verb for piercing in any case.
arguments.assessment: Neither side's strongest claim holds up. 'Deliberate Christian mistranslation' fails. The reading 'they dug' is the Septuagint's, which Kravitz himself explains as a translator's misunderstanding, not a Christian change, and at least one ancient Hebrew fragment is reported to read differently from the Masoretic text. 'Clear prophecy of crucifixion' also fails: the Masoretic reading is 'like a lion', the alternative means 'dug' rather than 'nailed', and the verse sits in a sequence of animal images. Kravitz's point that the Letter of Aristeas concerns only the Torah is accurate, but it does not settle the date of the Greek Psalter. The fair verdict is that the text of this one word is genuinely uncertain. The lion reading has the Masoretic tradition and the context behind it. The 'dug/pierced' reading has the Septuagint and possibly Nahal Hever. The verse cannot carry decisive weight for either side.

arguments.title: Does Jeremiah's 'new covenant' replace the Torah, or write the same Torah on Israel's heart?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Christian replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Maimonides (Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 9:1)
arguments.argument: Hebrews 8 quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 and concludes: 'In that he says, A new covenant, he has made the first old ... near to vanishing away' (8:13). Paul says believers 'have been discharged from the law' (Romans 7:6) and are 'no longer under a tutor' (Galatians 3:25). Rosenfeld answers that Jeremiah's new covenant is made 'with the House of Israel and the House of Judah'. Its content is that God will put 'My Torah' within them and write it on their hearts (31:33), so it is the same Torah, internalized rather than abolished. Israel broke the covenant (Jeremiah 11:10; Ezekiel 16:59), but God repeatedly promises not to annul it (Leviticus 26:44-45; Ezekiel 16:60). The Torah calls its commandments 'a law for all time throughout the ages' (e.g. Leviticus 23:14) and forbids adding to or subtracting from them (Deuteronomy 13:1). Maimonides draws the conclusion: anyone who says 'the mitzvot commanded to the Jews are not forever, but rather were given for a limited time' is a false prophet, even if he performs signs.

texts.note: 31:30 in some Jewish editions, as Rosenfeld notes; Sefaria uses 31:31
'I will put My Teaching (torati) into their inmost being'
chukkat olam, 'a law for all time'
12:32 in some editions
the slave serves le'olam, 'for life', showing olam can mean an open-ended but limited term
cited by Rosenfeld; not checked
cited by Rosenfeld; not checked

other_texts.ref: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 9:1

response_by: The Letter to the Hebrews and Paul (New Testament)
arguments.response: GotQuestions argues that the new covenant was foretold while the old was still in force. Moses foresaw God circumcising Israel's heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), Jeremiah promised the law written on the heart, and Ezekiel promised 'a new heart' and God's Spirit (36:26-27). Jesus is its mediator: at the Last Supper he called the cup 'the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20). 'Jesus Christ came to fulfill the Law of Moses (Matthew 5:17) and to establish the New Covenant ... The Old Covenant was written in stone, but the New Covenant is written on hearts.' Christians also point out that Jeremiah himself says the new covenant will 'not be like the covenant I made with their ancestors' (31:32), which is the phrase Hebrews builds on. They argue that Christianity claims to fulfil the law, not to destroy it (Matthew 5:17-18; Romans 3:31).
arguments.facts: Checkable: Jeremiah 31:31-33 promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the Exodus covenant, in which God's Torah will be written on hearts. The passage does not say the commandments are cancelled, and it does not mention Gentiles, a Messiah or sacrifice. Hebrews 8:13 reasons from the single word 'new' that the first covenant is becoming obsolete. Paul's statements about being released from the law are explicit. 'Olam' ('for all time') sometimes means a limited lifetime, as with the slave in Exodus 21:6. That weakens, but does not remove, arguments built on that word alone. Interpretation: whether 'not like the covenant' means different in content or different in durability (unbreakable, inward) is the crux.
arguments.assessment: On Jeremiah's own words the Jewish reading is the more natural one. The parties are Israel and Judah, the content is God's Torah, and the change is that it becomes inward and unbreakable. Nothing in the passage announces the end of the commandments. The Christian argument depends on reading Jeremiah through Hebrews and on the phrase 'not like the covenant', which is a real textual hook but does not specify abolition. The Christian claim to 'fulfil' rather than 'abolish' the law (Matthew 5:17) is consistent with its own texts, but Paul's language about release from the law (Romans 7:6) shows real discontinuity. The argument from 'olam' is weaker than often presented, because the word can denote limited permanence. Fair verdict: as an exegesis of Jeremiah 31 the Jewish case is strong. Whether the new covenant was inaugurated in Jesus depends on accepting the New Testament's interpretation, which this passage cannot establish by itself.

arguments.title: Does the Quran misplace Haman, the Persian official of Esther, in Pharaoh's court?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Abraham Geiger, 'Judaism and Islam' (1833; English translation 1898)
Theodor Noldeke, Josef Horovitz and Adam Silverstein (as quoted and summarized by Islamic Awareness)
arguments.argument: The Quran names Haman six times as a senior figure at the court of the Pharaoh of Moses (28:6, 28:8, 28:38, 29:39, 40:24, 40:36). Pharaoh tells him to 'ignite ... [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a tower that I may look at the God of Moses' (28:38; cf. 40:36-37). In the Hebrew Bible the only Haman is the enemy of the Jews at the Persian court of Ahasuerus (Esther 3:1), many centuries after Moses. The baked-brick tower reaching to heaven also recalls Babel (Genesis 11:3-4). Geiger, the 19th-century Jewish scholar, argued that 'Muhammad must at some time have heard him mentioned as the Jew's enemy, and therefore have put him in here.' Islamic Awareness quotes Noldeke: 'The most ignorant Jew could never have mistaken Haman (the minister of Ahasuerus) for the minister of the Pharaoh.' It also reports that Horovitz took a similar view and that Silverstein made the most detailed case for a literary transfer of Haman from Esther to the Quran.

texts.note: the baked bricks of Babel; not separately checked

response_by: Islamic Awareness ('Biblical Haman » Qur'anic Haman', 2000, updated 2012)
Muhammad Asad and Anthony Johns (Encyclopaedia of the Qur'an), as summarized in Wikipedia 'Haman (Islam)'
arguments.response: Islamic Awareness makes three points. First, the critics measure the Quran against the Book of Esther, yet most modern biblical scholars regard Esther as unhistorical. It quotes Adele Berlin: 'Very few twentieth-century Bible scholars believed in the historicity of the book of Esther'. Second, the Quranic Haman is a distinct character: an official in charge of building who belongs to Pharaoh's inner circle, with no parallel to the Esther plot. Third, it surveys Egyptian lexicons, which list ḤMN as the name of a god used in priestly titles, and suggests that Haman may be a title connected to a senior priest. Wikipedia reports that Muhammad Asad identified the name with a supposed Egyptian title 'Ha-Amen', a high priest. It also reports that Anthony Johns, author of the Encyclopaedia of the Qur'an entry, suggested the name may have been used for 'any anti-Jewish court official'.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the Quran places a Haman with Pharaoh and Moses and has him commissioned to fire clay for a tower. Esther 3:1 places Haman at the Persian court. Wikipedia states that 'There is no evidence of such stories in Egyptian history.' Islamic Awareness's own lexicon survey reports that Ranke's dictionary of Egyptian personal names lists no names under HMN, so its title hypothesis rests on the ḤMN deity element in priestly titles, not on any attested official named Haman. Interpretation: whether the Quran borrowed from Esther, used a title, or refers to an otherwise unknown person cannot be settled from the texts.
arguments.assessment: The Jewish and academic argument is strong as a probability argument. The only Haman known from earlier literature is a Persian-era enemy of the Jews, and the tower motif echoes Babel, so a conflation is the simplest explanation. The Muslim replies show that the conflation is not proven. The Quranic Haman is a different character, the Quran does not claim to retell Esther, and absence of evidence from Egypt is not proof of error. But the title hypothesis is a construction with no direct attestation. The Esther-historicity point does not make an Egyptian Haman any more likely, because the objection depends only on the name being otherwise attested in Persia, not on Esther being history. Fair verdict: the anachronism charge is stronger than the replies, but it rests on inference, not on a decisive contradiction.

arguments.title: Who made the golden calf: Aaron, as Exodus says, or 'the Samiri', as the Quran says?

favours.text: Evenly balanced: each side has real texts on its side, and neither has disproved the other.

by: Abraham Geiger, 'Judaism and Islam' (1833; English translation 1898)
Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Calf, Golden', section 'Samiri's Identity with Samael'
arguments.argument: In Exodus, Aaron casts the calf (32:4). He later tells Moses 'I hurled it into the fire and out came this calf' (32:24), and the narrator speaks of 'the calf that Aaron made' (32:35). In the Quran, Aaron warns the people against it (20:90; cf. 7:150, 20:94), and the calf is produced by al-Samiri (20:85-88, 95-97), who is condemned to say 'No contact'. Jewish scholars see this as a figure assembled from later material. Geiger suggested 'Perhaps Muhammad formed the word Samiri from a confusion with the name Samael'. He drew on the rabbinic tradition that Sammael entered the calf and made it low (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45). He also noted that 'Samiri was the name for Samaritan'. The Jewish Encyclopedia, citing Frankel and Hosea 8:5 ('your calf, Samaria'), says Muhammad 'made the seducer a Samaritan in spite of all chronology'. Samaria was founded by Omri and named after Shemer (1 Kings 16:24), centuries after Moses, and the northern kingdom's golden calves were proclaimed with the very words of Exodus 32:4 ('This is your god, O Israel, who brought you up from Egypt', 1 Kings 12:28).

texts.note: JPS notes the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain

other_texts.note: 'Rabbi Jehudah said: Sammael entered into it, and he was lowing to mislead Israel'

response_by: Islamic Awareness ('The "Samaritan" Error In The Qur'an?', 1999, updated 2013)
Abdullah Yusuf Ali (as quoted by Gleason Archer, cited by Islamic Awareness)
arguments.response: Islamic Awareness argues that the charge confuses two words. Shomronim in 2 Kings 17:29 means inhabitants of the city or region of Samaria. The Samaritans 'do not address themselves by this name at all. They call themselves shamerin, that is "keepers" or "observers" of the Torah.' It cites the Encyclopaedia Judaica, James Montgomery and the Samaritan Chronicle II for this distinction, so al-Samiri need not imply the city Omri built. Yusuf Ali suggested Egyptian 'stranger' or Hebrew shomer, 'watchman'. Islamic Awareness also argues that Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer was finally redacted after the rise of Islam, so it cannot be a source of the Quran. On Aaron, the Muslim position is that the Quran corrects the biblical portrait of a prophet as an idol-maker. The Quran shows Aaron resisting the people under threat ('the people oppressed me and were about to kill me', 7:150).
arguments.facts: Checkable: Exodus says Aaron cast the calf. The Quran says the Samiri produced it while Aaron objected. These are direct contradictions between the two accounts. The Quran never says the Samiri came from Samaria; the meaning of the epithet is the disputed point. 1 Kings 16:24 dates the city name Samaria to Omri. The calf formula of Exodus 32:4 recurs at 1 Kings 12:28, and Hosea speaks of 'the calf of Samaria'. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45 has Sammael inside the calf. Its post-Islamic final redaction is asserted by Islamic Awareness and I did not check it independently. Interpretation: whether 'Samiri' is a Samaritan, a Samarian, a garbled Samael or a personal epithet cannot be settled from the Quran's text.
arguments.assessment: The anachronism form of the argument ('there were no Samaritans in Moses' day') is weaker than critics often present it. The Quran gives an epithet, not a place of origin, and the Samaritans' own name for themselves offers a non-anachronistic sense. The literary echoes are real, though: a calf, a figure whose name sounds like Samaria or Samael, and a tradition of a supernatural agent animating the calf. They make a dependence on Israelite and rabbinic material a reasonable hypothesis, but not a proven one, especially as the key rabbinic parallel may be later. The clear difference over Aaron is a disagreement between scriptures, not an error that either side can show from neutral evidence. Fair verdict: the Jewish objection points to real tensions, but its strongest version is unproven, and the Muslim reply is adequate on 'Samaritan' and question-begging on Aaron, as is the Jewish side.

arguments.title: Is Quran 5:32 ('whoever kills a soul ... as if he had slain mankind') taken from the Mishnah?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Abraham Geiger, 'Judaism and Islam' (1833; English translation 1898)
arguments.argument: After telling of Cain and Abel, the raven that shows the killer how to hide the body (5:31), the Quran says: 'Because of that, We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely' (5:32). Geiger observed that 'One perceives here no connection at all, if one does not consider the following Hebrew passage': Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. There the Mishnah derives exactly this teaching from the Cain story. Genesis 4:10 says 'your brother's bloods', in the plural, meaning Abel and all his unborn descendants, and the Mishnah adds that Adam was created alone to teach that destroying one life is like destroying a whole world and saving one is like saving a whole world. The 'because of that' link is a piece of rabbinic exegesis, not anything in the Torah. Geiger concludes that 'he had evidently received this rule from his informants when they related to him this particular event.' He also traced the raven to Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 21, where a raven teaches Adam how to bury Abel.

texts.note: printed Hebrew text reads nefesh achat miYisrael, 'one soul from Israel'
quoted within the Mishnah; not separately fetched
'The birds of the heavens and the kosher beasts buried him'

other_texts.note: same teaching without 'from Israel'
a raven buries its fellow and Adam copies it
two clean birds; Cain learns burial from them

response_by: Islamic Awareness ('On The Sources Of The Story Of Cain & Abel In The Qur'an', 1998, updated 2006)
arguments.response: Islamic Awareness replies that the Quran itself says this ruling was 'decreed upon the Children of Israel', so its presence in Jewish tradition is what the Quran would lead one to expect. It also notes real differences. The Quran adds the exception 'unless for a soul or for corruption in the land', and it speaks of any soul, whereas standard printed texts of the Mishnah say 'one soul from Israel'. The page also notes that Geiger and Tisdall quoted different versions of the Mishnah. On the raven, it argues that Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer and the Tanhuma reached their final form after Islam, and it quotes Norman Stillman: 'what was thought to be a Jewish haggadic influence in an Islamic text might well be quite the reverse.' Ibn Kathir explains 'We decreed' as 'We legislated for them and informed them'. He reads the verse as a lesson that 'there is no difference between one life and another', without reference to Jewish texts.
arguments.facts: Checkable: Quran 5:32 and Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 share the same structure (one life equals a whole world, for both killing and saving), and both attach it to the Cain story. The Mishnah, compiled around 200 CE, predates the Quran. The Hebrew Bible contains no such decree, so the parallel is with rabbinic teaching, not scripture. The Sefaria Hebrew Mishnah reads 'from Israel'; the Jerusalem Talmud's version of the same passage does not. Bird-burial traditions appear in Bereshit Rabbah 22:8 (birds bury Abel), Tanhuma Bereshit 10 (a bird teaches Cain) and Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 21 (a raven teaches Adam). Their dates relative to the Quran differ and I did not verify them. Interpretation: whether the Quran 'took' the teaching or confirms a decree it says was given to Israel depends on prior belief about revelation.
arguments.assessment: The parallel is real and close, and the Jewish argument correctly identifies its source type. The Quran's 'We decreed upon the Children of Israel' matches a rabbinic deduction from Genesis 4:10, not any verse of the Torah, and that explains the otherwise abrupt 'because of that'. This is the strongest of the 'Jewish sources of the Quran' arguments. The Muslim reply blunts but does not remove it. The Quran explicitly attributes the teaching to what was given to Israel, and 'decreed' need not mean 'written in the Torah'. The Quranic version also differs in wording and scope. The raven part of the argument is weaker, because the closest parallel (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer) may be later than the Quran, although Bereshit Rabbah's birds and the Tanhuma show the motif existed in some form. Fair verdict: the texts show the Quran echoes a specific rabbinic teaching. Whether that reflects human borrowing or confirmation by revelation cannot be decided from the texts.

arguments.title: Does Daniel 9 require the Messiah to come and die before the Second Temple was destroyed?

favours.text: On this question the Christian side makes more sense on the texts. The Jewish replies have not overturned it so far.

by: Michael L. Brown, 'Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus', vol. 3 (2003), as quoted by judaismsanswer.com
arguments.argument: Daniel 9:24 decrees 'seventy weeks' to finish transgression, expiate iniquity, bring everlasting righteousness, seal vision and prophet, and anoint the holy of holies. Verse 25 counts from 'the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem' to an 'anointed leader'. Verse 26 says that after sixty-two weeks 'the anointed one will be cut off', and then a coming leader's people 'will destroy the city and the sanctuary'. The Romans destroyed the city and Temple in 70 CE. Brown, as quoted by his Jewish critic, writes: 'Since Daniel 9:24-27 speaks of events that must be fulfilled before the destruction of the Second Temple (which took place in 70 CE), the question that must be asked is this: If Jesus did not fulfill Daniel 9:24, who did?' On this reading an anointed figure dies before the destruction, which fits Jesus, crucified some forty years earlier.

texts.note: Hebrew accent (etnachta) falls after 'seven weeks', separating it from 'sixty-two weeks'
mashiach without the definite article, in both 9:25 and 9:26
Cyrus called God's 'anointed'
'the anointed priest'

response_by: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld (Aish.com, drawing on Tovia Singer)
judaismsanswer.com (anonymous Jewish author responding to Brown)
arguments.response: Rashi identifies the 'anointed leader' of 9:25 as Cyrus, whom Isaiah 45:1 calls God's anointed. He identifies the one 'cut off' in 9:26 as 'Agrippa, the king of Judea, who was ruling at the time of the destruction', and remarks that mashiach here 'is purely an expression of a prince and a dignitary'. Rosenfeld argues that the passage speaks of two different anointed persons, one after seven weeks and another after sixty-two weeks. The term mashiach is used throughout the Bible for kings and priests. On the Christian view the Messiah is cut off in the middle of the final 'week' and the Temple falls at its end, but Jesus 'was crucified in the early 30's C.E. which was well over the half week (3.5 years) before the Temple's destruction in the year 70'. The judaismsanswer author argues that 9:24 is addressed to 'your people and your holy city'. On this view the six goals are tasks set before the nation, and the destruction of the Temple shows they were not achieved, so they need not have been fulfilled by an individual before 70 CE.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the order in 9:26 is that an anointed one is cut off and then city and sanctuary are destroyed. Rashi also applies the verse to the Roman destruction (Titus). In the Masoretic text the major accent divides 'seven weeks' from 'sixty-two weeks', as the JPS translation shows. Christian translations that add them into sixty-nine weeks before 'Messiah the Prince' depart from that accentuation. Neither occurrence of mashiach has the article, and the word denotes kings and priests elsewhere (Isaiah 45:1; Leviticus 4:3). The starting point of the count ('the issuance of the word') and the length of the years are not specified in the text. Interpretation: identifying the anointed one with Jesus requires choices of starting date and calendar that the passage does not fix.
arguments.assessment: Brown's argument has a genuine textual anchor. Daniel 9 links an anointed figure's being 'cut off' with the destruction of city and sanctuary, and both Jewish and Christian readers place that destruction in 70 CE. That makes the passage a fair challenge to any reading that ignores the Second Temple period. But the argument does not show that the figure must be the Messiah. The word is used for any anointed ruler or priest, Rashi offers a historical candidate (Agrippa), and the traditional Christian chronology runs the two time periods together against the Hebrew accents. Brown's question 'who else fulfilled 9:24?' assumes the six goals had to be completed by one person before 70 CE, which the text does not say. Fair verdict: suggestive but not demonstrative. It shows Christians are not inventing a Second Temple setting, but the identification with Jesus depends on contested chronology.

arguments.title: Is the child of Isaiah 9:6 called 'Mighty God', and is he the Messiah or King Hezekiah?

favours.text: Evenly balanced: each side has real texts on its side, and neither has disproved the other.

arguments.argument: Isaiah 9:6-7 (9:5-6 in Hebrew) announces a child born to rule 'on the throne of David' with peace 'without end', and gives him the names Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God (El Gibbor), Everlasting Father and Prince of Peace. McLatchie argues the child is the Messiah. Isaiah 11 describes the same Davidic ruler, and the parallel prophecies in Micah 5 and Zechariah 9 point the same way. Matthew applies Isaiah 9:1-2 to Jesus (Matthew 4:14-16). The Aramaic Targum Jonathan also reads the passage as messianic. He answers the Hezekiah objection directly. 'El Gibbor' is unequivocally a title of the God of Israel in Isaiah 10:21. Hezekiah's son Manasseh was a wicked idolater, so Hezekiah's line did not bring endless peace. The past-tense verbs are a prophetic perfect, a device Isaiah uses elsewhere to describe future events as already done. The child therefore bears a divine title, which Christians see fulfilled in Jesus.

texts.note: 'a remnant of Jacob, to Mighty God (El Gibbor)'

other_texts.note: verbs yullad, nittan, vattehi, vayyiqra are perfect/past forms

arguments.response: Singer, as quoted by McLatchie, writes: 'This verse is not discussing any future event or the messiah. Rather, Isaiah is describing the exaltation of King Hezekiah and the divine names bestowed upon him following the miracle when Jerusalem was saved from the Assyrian siege.' He adds that Christian Bibles 'changed all of the past tense verbs ... into a future tense'. Rashi reads the names as describing the one who gives the name: 'The Holy One, blessed be He, Who gives wondrous counsel, is a mighty God and an everlasting Father, called Hezekiah's name, "the prince of peace"'. The JPS translation renders the whole as a sentence-name: 'The Mighty God is planning grace; The Eternal Father, a peaceable ruler'. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 94a) links the verse to Hezekiah, saying God 'sought to designate King Hezekiah as the Messiah' but did not, because Hezekiah failed to sing God's praise.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the Hebrew verbs are past forms, so the issue is whether they are a prophetic perfect. The four titles can be read grammatically as names of the child or as a sentence about God given as the child's name. El Gibbor is a title of God in Isaiah 10:21. Targum Jonathan does apply the passage to the Messiah, as McLatchie says. But it assigns the divine titles to the namer, not the child: 'His name is called from before Him who is wonderful in counsel, the mighty God who liveth to eternity - the Messiah whose peace shall be great'. Sanhedrin 94a ties the verse to Hezekiah as a would-be Messiah. 2 Kings 18:5 praises Hezekiah's trust, and 2 Kings 21:2 records that his son Manasseh did evil.
arguments.assessment: Each side wins one half of the argument. The Christian side is strong that the passage describes an ideal Davidic king with endless rule, more than any historical king of Judah achieved. Jewish sources themselves (Targum Jonathan; the Talmud's 'would-be Messiah' Hezekiah) read it in messianic terms. The Jewish side is strong that the grammar does not force the divine titles onto the child: Rashi and, notably, the Targum McLatchie cites both take them as describing God who names him. Singer's charge that the verbs were 'changed' overstates the case, since the prophetic perfect is a recognised Hebrew usage, but his reading is also grammatically possible. Fair verdict: the messianic reading is well supported, but the claim that the passage calls the Messiah God is possible, not established.

arguments.title: In Zechariah 12:10, is God the one who is 'pierced', and does the Talmud apply the verse to a slain Messiah?

favours.text: Evenly balanced: each side has real texts on its side, and neither has disproved the other.

arguments.argument: In Zechariah 12:10 God speaks: 'they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son'. GotQuestions argues the prediction is 'amazing because it is God Himself speaking - the Lord is the One who is pierced'. It notes that John applies the verse to the spear wound at the crucifixion (John 19:37) and Revelation to Christ's return (Revelation 1:7). It also links the 'only son' and 'firstborn' language to Jesus as God's only Son. Christians add that the Talmud itself applies the verse to a slain Messiah. In Sukkah 52a, one sage says the end-time mourning of Zechariah 12 is 'for Messiah ben Yosef who was killed', and cites 'they shall look unto Me because they have thrust him through'.

texts.note: Hebrew ve-hibbitu elai et asher-daqaru ve-safedu alav

other_texts.note: known to me only as quoted by Rashi; English not available on Sefaria

other_texts.ref: Michael Brown, Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus vol. 3 p. 49
other_texts.note: cited in a search summary as discussing this verse and Alshich; not read

arguments.response: Rashi reads: 'they shall look to Me because of those who have been thrust through' - Israel will turn to God 'to complain about those of them whom the nations thrust through and slew during their exile'. 'They shall mourn over it' means 'over that slaughter'. He quotes Targum Jonathan: 'they shall supplicate Me because of their wanderings'. The JPS translation likewise has 'they shall lament to Me about those who are slain'. The switch from 'me' to 'him' shows that the one mourned is distinct from God. Rashi openly records the Talmud's view: 'our Sages expounded this in tractate Sukkah (52a) as referring to the Messiah, son of Joseph, who was slain'. But in Sukkah 52a that figure is killed in the war of Gog and Magog before the final redemption, and the Talmud records a second opinion that the mourning is 'for the evil inclination that was killed'.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the Hebrew has God speaking ('to me'), then 'et asher daqaru' (whom / concerning whom they pierced), then 'mourn for him'. The pronoun shifts from first to third person, which both sides must explain. Sukkah 52a records a dispute: one view applies the verse to Messiah ben Yosef, killed in the war of Gog and Magog, and the other to the evil inclination. John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 apply the verse to Jesus. Interpretation: whether 'et asher' is in apposition to 'me' (God is the pierced one) or introduces a separate object (look to me concerning the one pierced) is the grammatical crux.
arguments.assessment: The Christian argument scores a real point: a messianic reading of Zechariah 12:10, including a slain messianic figure, is attested in the Talmud and acknowledged by Rashi, so it is not merely a Christian invention. But the Talmudic figure is a warrior-Messiah killed in an end-time war, which is different from Jesus' story, and the Talmud gives an alternative non-messianic reading. The stronger claim that God himself is pierced rests on one possible construal of an ambiguous construction. The 'me ... him' shift is at least as easily read as distinguishing the pierced one from God. Fair verdict: the Christian case is good evidence that the verse was read messianically, and weak evidence that it teaches a pierced God.

arguments.title: Was the son Abraham was told to sacrifice Ishmael, the 'only son' for fourteen years, rather than Isaac?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim argument has not shown what it claims.

by: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi (as reported by Ibn Kathir)
arguments.argument: Genesis 22:2 says 'Take your son, your only son ... Isaac'. Ishmael was born when Abraham was 86 (Genesis 16:16) and Isaac when he was 100 (Genesis 21:5), so for about fourteen years Ishmael was Abraham's only son. Ibn Kathir argues that the words 'only son' 'cannot be said except in the case of one who has no other son', and that the Jews 'falsely inserted the name of Ishaq ... because he is their ancestor, while Isma'il is the ancestor of the Arabs'. In the Quran, the story of the sacrifice of the 'forbearing boy' (37:101-107) is followed by 'And We gave him good tidings of Isaac' (37:112). Al-Qurazi argued that God had already promised Isaac a son, Jacob (11:71), so he would not have commanded Isaac's sacrifice: 'The one whom He commanded him to sacrifice can only have been Isma'il.'

texts.note: Hebrew et-yechidcha ... et-Yitzchak; JPS renders 'your favored one'
Abraham was 100, not 99 as the English Ibn Kathir has it

other_texts.note: citing Genesis Rabbah 55:7 and Sanhedrin 89b

response_by: Early Muslim scholars including al-Tabari and Ibn Qutaybah (as summarized in Wikipedia 'Binding of Isaac')
arguments.response: Jewish tradition already discussed the 'only son' difficulty. Rashi records the midrash: 'Abraham said to God, "I have two sons". He answered him, "Thine only son". Abraham said, "This one is the only son of his mother and the other is the only son of his mother". God then said, "the one whom thou lovest". Abraham replied, "I love both of them". Whereupon God said "even Isaac".' Genesis itself prepares for this. God says 'it is through Isaac that offspring shall be continued for you' (21:12), and the covenant is established with Isaac (17:19, 21). Ishmael had already been sent away (21:14) before chapter 22. So 'your only one' refers to the one son left with Abraham and designated heir. The Quran does not name the son in Surah 37. Wikipedia reports that early Muslim scholars disputed his identity: al-Tabari and Ibn Qutaybah held it was Isaac, although most Muslims today hold it was Ishmael.
arguments.facts: Checkable: the name Isaac stands in the Hebrew of Genesis 22:2, and Ibn Kathir offers no manuscript evidence for its insertion. Genesis gives the ages he cites (86 and 100) and sends Ishmael away before the binding. The word yachid ('only', 'unique') is used, and JPS renders it 'favored one'. Quran 37:101-107 does not name the son; 37:112 announces Isaac after the episode. Interpretation: whether 'only son' can mean the remaining or uniquely beloved son, and whether the order in Surah 37 implies two different sons, are readings, not facts.
arguments.assessment: The Muslim argument has surface force, because 'your only son' is awkward when Abraham has two sons. Jewish exegesis felt that awkwardness and answered it long ago. Within Genesis the answer is coherent: Ishmael has been sent away and Isaac is the named covenant heir. The charge that 'Isaac' was inserted has no textual evidence behind it. The Quranic argument from the order of 37:101-112 is a reasonable reading of the Quran, but it is not decisive, as shown by the early Muslim scholars who identified the son as Isaac. Fair verdict: each scripture can be read consistently on its own terms. The specific claim of Jewish tampering with Genesis 22 is weak.

arguments.title: Does 'He shone forth from Mount Paran' (Deuteronomy 33:2) foretell Muhammad in Mecca?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim argument has not shown what it claims.

by: Jamal Badawi (IslamOnline, 'Muhammad in the Bible - Location')
Khalil Ahmad Nasir, 'Muhammad in the Bible' (Ahmadiyya Muslim Community)
arguments.argument: Deuteronomy 33:2 says the LORD 'came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints: from his right hand went a fiery law' (KJV wording, as quoted by Nasir). Nasir reads three manifestations: Sinai for Moses, Seir for Jesus and Paran for Muhammad. Ishmael 'dwelt in the wilderness of Paran' (Genesis 21:21), and Paran (Arabic Faran) is identified with the hills of Mecca. The 'ten thousands of saints' are those who entered Mecca with Muhammad, and the 'fiery law' is the Quran. Badawi argues that Paran cannot be Sinai, since Sinai is already named and Genesis 14:6 and Numbers 10:12 distinguish them. He adds that Arab geographers (he cites Mu'jam al-Buldan) used Faran for Mecca and that Habakkuk 3:3 ('the Holy One from Mount Paran') points the same way.

texts.note: JPS takes Ribeboth-kodesh as a place name; KJV 'ten thousands of saints'
'Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran'
travellers go from Midian to Paran and on to Egypt

other_texts.note: citing Sifrei Devarim 343 and Avodah Zarah 2b
cited by Badawi; not checked

response_by: The Hebrew Bible's own geography of Paran (Numbers 10:12, 13:3, 13:26; 1 Kings 11:18)
arguments.response: Jewish tradition also links Seir and Paran to Esau and Ishmael, but in the opposite sense. Rashi, following Sifrei, says God 'first addressed Himself to the sons of Esau ... that they should accept the Law, but they refused'. He then 'went there and addressed Himself to the sons of Ishmael (who dwelt in Paran, see Genesis 21:21) that they should accept it and they also refused', and so came to Israel. On geography, the Bible places the wilderness of Paran on Israel's route from Sinai: the cloud settles there after Sinai (Numbers 10:12), the spies are sent from it, and Kadesh is 'in the wilderness of Paran' (13:26). Paran also lies on the road from Midian to Egypt (1 Kings 11:18). That places it in the Sinai-Negev region, far from Mecca. The verbs of 33:2 are past ('came', 'shone', 'appeared') and introduce Moses' blessing of the tribes. Parallel poems (Judges 5:4, Habakkuk 3:3) also describe God marching from the southern regions of Seir, Edom, Teman and Paran in a single theophany.
arguments.facts: Checkable: Deuteronomy 33:2 names Sinai, Seir and Mount Paran in a poem about God's coming, using past-tense verbs, before the blessings of the tribes. Ishmael lived in 'the wilderness of Paran' (Genesis 21:21), and his mother found him a wife from Egypt. The Bible's other references put Paran between Sinai and Kadesh and between Midian and Egypt. Rashi connects Paran to Ishmael but as those who refused the Torah. The 'ten thousands of saints' depends on a translation; JPS reads a place name. Not checked: the Arab geographers' use of Faran for Mecca.
arguments.assessment: The argument's strongest point is real: Paran is the land of Ishmael in Genesis, and even rabbinic tradition associates Paran with Ishmael's descendants. Everything else depends on identifying biblical Paran with Mecca, and the Bible's own geography does not support that. Its Paran is a wilderness on the Exodus route containing Kadesh and lying between Midian and Egypt. The reading of three successive prophets also strains a poem that describes one past theophany in the southern regions, as Judges 5 and Habakkuk 3 do. The '10,000' detail rests on the KJV rendering. Badawi's point that Paran is distinct from Sinai is correct, but it shows only that Paran is another place in the same region. Fair verdict: weak as a prophecy argument, though the Jewish reply should concede that Paran's Ishmaelite associations are genuinely biblical and rabbinic.

arguments.title: Does the Bible admit the Torah was corrupted ('the lying pen of the scribes', Jeremiah 8:8)?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim argument has not shown what it claims.

arguments.argument: The Quran accuses some People of the Book of distorting words 'from their [proper] usages' (4:46, 5:13). It says some 'distort the Torah after they had understood it' (2:75), 'alter the Scripture with their tongues' (3:78), and 'write the "scripture" with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah"' (2:79). Wilson argues that the Bible itself confirms this. Jeremiah 8:8 says 'How do you say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? But, behold, the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie'. Wilson notes that the Hebrew word is Torah and comments 'what is stated is crystal clear'. He adds that 2 Kings 22:8 has the high priest 'find the book of the law' in Josiah's day. Citing Edgar Goodspeed, he says this was the discovery of Deuteronomy in 621 BC, which implies the Torah had been lost. He also points to books the Bible cites that no longer exist, such as the Book of the Wars of the LORD (Numbers 21:14) and the Book of Jasher (Joshua 10:13).

texts.note: Hebrew lasheqer asah et sheqer sofrim; WEB 'the false pen of the scribes has worked falsely'; JPS 'for naught has the pen labored'
cited by Wilson; not checked
cited by Wilson; not checked

other_texts.note: Hebrew only on Sefaria; read in Hebrew

response_by: Maimonides (Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10, eighth principle)
arguments.response: Jewish commentators read Jeremiah 8:8 as an attack on people who possess the Torah but do not keep it, not as a statement that its text was changed. Radak explains: if the Torah of God is with you and you do not fulfil it, then whoever made the pen to write it made it in vain, and the scribes wrote it in vain, for since you do not keep it, it is as if it were not written. He takes lasheqer to mean 'in vain'. Rashi identifies the 'false pen of the scribes' as 'your prophet', meaning the false prophets. The next verse supports this: 'they reject the word of GOD, so their wisdom amounts to nothing' (8:9). 2 Kings 22:8 says a scroll was found, which presupposes that it already existed. The rabbis were not hiding difficulties: the Talmud openly discusses who wrote the account of Moses' death (Deuteronomy 34:5) and records a view that Joshua wrote the last eight verses (Bava Batra 15a). Maimonides states that 'this Torah that is given to us through Moshe ... is completely from the mouth of the Almighty'. Jewish respondents also point out that the Quran tells Jews they 'have the Torah, in which is the judgement of Allah' (5:43) and challenges them to 'bring the Torah and recite it' (3:93).
arguments.facts: Checkable: Jeremiah 8:8's Hebrew can be rendered 'made it into a lie' or 'labored in vain/falsely'. It does not say that scribes altered the words of the Torah, and its context (8:9) concerns rejecting God's word. 2 Kings 22:8 reports finding a Torah scroll in the Temple. The Quranic verses accuse some People of the Book of distortion and of writing texts themselves. The Quran also presupposes that a Torah containing God's judgement was in Jewish hands (5:43). Interpretation: whether the Quranic accusations concern the text or its meaning is disputed within Islam (see the existing entry on tahrif). Modern critical scholarship's view of Deuteronomy, which Wilson cites via Goodspeed, is a separate question from Jeremiah 8:8.
arguments.assessment: As an argument that the Torah confesses its own corruption, this is weak. Jeremiah 8:8 is ambiguous, its context points to false teaching and disobedience, and Jeremiah elsewhere treats the Torah as authoritative. 2 Kings 22 describes rediscovery, not loss of the text. Lost books mentioned in the Bible are not books of the Torah. Wilson's stronger material comes from modern critical scholarship on how Deuteronomy was composed, which does challenge traditional Mosaic authorship. But that scholarship rests on methods that would apply equally to the Quran's account of Moses, and it does not show the deliberate tampering the Quran's critics of tahrif have in mind. The Jewish reply is solid on Jeremiah. The Quran's own references to a Torah 'in which is the judgement of Allah' make a total-corruption claim hard to sustain from the Quran itself. Fair verdict: weak argument; the debate is better conducted on the Quranic verses than on Jeremiah.

arguments.title: Is Israel's election permanent, or did the Quran rightly make it conditional and open to all?

favours.text: On this question the Jewish side makes more sense on the texts. The Muslim argument has not shown what it claims.

by: Louay Fatoohi (Yaqeen Institute, 'Who Are the Chosen Ones? The Qur'an's Correction of the Bible on the Election of the Children of Israel', 2024)
arguments.argument: The Quran affirms that God 'preferred you over the worlds' (2:47, 2:122; 45:16), but it attaches conditions. Israel must fulfil its covenant (2:40; 5:12). For breaking it they were cursed (5:13). God's covenant with Abraham's line 'does not include the wrongdoers' (2:124). The claim 'We are the children of Allah and His beloved' is answered with 'Then why does He punish you for your sins?' (5:18; cf. 62:6). Fatoohi argues that the Hebrew Bible 'presents the Israelites as God's exclusive people, whom He loved more than any other nation and has an eternal covenant with. Yet it fails to give a meaningful explanation of this chosenness or justify it.' He points out a tension: the Sinai covenant is conditional on obedience, yet Israel 'would never lose their status as His chosen.' The Quran, he says, 'corrects' this. God chose Israel 'as a host nation of prophets and the guardians of prophetic heritage'. The 'best nation' (3:110) is now open to anyone who follows God's commands through the Prophet Muhammad.
response_by: The Hebrew Bible's own explanations of election (Deuteronomy 7:7-8, 9:5; Exodus 19:5-6; Amos 3:2; Isaiah 42:6)
arguments.response: The Jewish reply is that the Hebrew Bible does explain election, and explains it as love and vocation, not merit or ethnic superiority. Israel was chosen not because it was numerous (Deuteronomy 7:7) or virtuous (9:5), but because 'GOD favored you and kept the oath made to your fathers' (7:8). Its purpose is to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation' (Exodus 19:6) and 'a light of nations' (Isaiah 42:6). Election brings stricter judgement, not immunity: 'You alone have I singled out ... That is why I will call you to account for all your iniquities' (Amos 3:2). The covenant can bring punishment, but God says he will not annul it even in exile (Leviticus 26:44; Jeremiah 31:35-36). Jews say this is a deliberate teaching that God's faithfulness outlasts Israel's failures, not an incoherence. Chosenness does not exclude others. The Mishnah says 'Beloved is man for he was created in the image [of God]' before speaking of Israel (Avot 3:14). Maimonides teaches that righteous Gentiles who keep the seven Noahide commandments 'merit a share in the world to come' (Kings 8:11). Outsiders can join Israel, as Ruth does ('your people shall be my people', Ruth 1:16).
arguments.facts: Checkable: both scriptures affirm that God chose and favoured Israel. The Hebrew Bible contains conditional language (Exodus 19:5, 'if you will obey Me') alongside promises of permanence (Leviticus 26:44; Jeremiah 31:35-36), so Fatoohi correctly identifies both strands. It also gives explicit reasons for election (love and the oath to the patriarchs, Deuteronomy 7:8) and a purpose (Exodus 19:6; Isaiah 42:6), so the claim that it 'fails to give' any explanation is not accurate as stated. The Quran attaches conditions and rejects claims of exclusive divine favour (5:18; 62:6). Interpretation: whether permanence despite disobedience is incoherent, or is an expression of covenant faithfulness, is a theological judgement.
arguments.assessment: The Muslim argument correctly identifies a real tension in the Hebrew Bible between conditional and unconditional language, and the Quran offers a tidy resolution. But it overstates its case when it says the Bible gives no explanation: Deuteronomy, Exodus, Amos and Isaiah offer reasons and a purpose, even if Fatoohi finds them unsatisfying. The Jewish reply answers the charge of ethnic privilege fairly well. Election entails accountability (Amos 3:2), converts can join, and rabbinic law gives righteous Gentiles a place in the world to come. It does not remove the particularism of a covenant with one people. Fair verdict: neither side is refuted. The disagreement is about whether God's covenant with Israel can survive Israel's disobedience. Each scripture answers that consistently on its own terms, and the texts alone cannot decide between them.
